Fort Sumter. A federal garrison in Charleston Harbor, South Carolina, this fort was the site of the opening engagement of the American Civil War on April twelfth and thirteenth, eighteen sixty-one. The Confederate government, freshly independent, demanded the Union's evacuation of the fort. When the Union refused to relinquish it, Confederate artillery bombarded it for thirty-four hours. The federal garrison, commanded by Major Robert Anderson, surrendered after the fort's magazines were exhausted. Though there were no combat deaths, the attack on the fort electrified both North and South, transformed political conflict into armed warfare, and solidified Union public opinion behind Lincoln's call for volunteers to suppress the rebellion.

South Carolina seceded in December eighteen sixty. As a newly independent state, it inherited federal forts and arsenals within its borders. Fort Sumter remained a Union garrison, becoming a symbol of federal authority in the seceded states. Lincoln, newly inaugurated, decided to resupply the isolated garrison with provisions.

Confederate General Pierre Beauregard issued an ultimatum to evacuate. Major Anderson refused. Confederate forces encircling the harbor—approximately six thousand troops—opened fire at dawn on April twelfth with artillery from Fort Moultrie and other batteries. After thirty-four hours of bombardment, Anderson's small garrison, about eighty soldiers, returned fire but could not resist. Anderson surrendered on April thirteenth.

The attack killed no one in combat, though two Confederate soldiers died in accidents during the bombardment. Lincoln called for seventy-five thousand volunteers to suppress the rebellion. This prompted further secessions and mobilization on both sides.

Fort Sumter transformed a constitutional crisis into a shooting war. The fort's isolation and symbolic importance made it the inevitable flashpoint. Both Lincoln and Jefferson Davis understood that whoever fired first would bear the political cost of initiating violence. Lincoln masterfully positioned himself to respond defensively, not aggressively, to the Confederate attack. The rapid mobilization following Sumter demonstrated both sides' willingness to fight and their confidence in quick victory—a confidence that would prove tragically wrong. The bombardment remains the symbolic beginning of American fratricide.
